title: Downtown in 1962: When Every Town Had a Department Store

scenes.text: It's a Saturday in December, nineteen sixty-two. Downtown is packed. Shoppers in wool coats and hats crowd the sidewalks. A Salvation Army bell is ringing on the corner. And in the middle of the main street stands the biggest building in town, with tall windows full of lights and moving figures. The department store.
scenes.caption: DECEMBER, 1962

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty-two, almost every American city and many small towns had at least one big department store downtown. In New York, Macy's and Gimbels. In Chicago, Marshall Field's. In Philadelphia, Wanamaker's. In Detroit, Hudson's. And in hundreds of smaller cities, a family-owned store with the founder's name carved over the door.
scenes.caption: EVERY TOWN HAD ONE

scenes.text: So let's go shopping. Let's walk through the doors of a downtown department store in nineteen sixty-two, and ride the elevator from the bargain basement all the way up to the tearoom on the top floor. If you remember those stores, I think you'll feel that warm air hit you as the revolving door spins.
scenes.caption: LET'S GO SHOPPING

scenes.text: Before you even went inside, there were the windows. In December, the big department stores competed to have the most magical Christmas windows in town. Mechanical elves hammered toys. Animated bears skated on mirror ponds. Snow fell on tiny villages. Families came downtown just to walk past the windows, and children pressed their noses against the glass.
scenes.query: 1960s department store Christmas window display children
scenes.caption: THE CHRISTMAS WINDOWS

scenes.text: Window dressers were artists. They worked for months on the holiday displays, and changed the windows every few weeks the rest of the year. Spring fashions, back-to-school clothes, summer beachwear. For many shoppers, the window was the first place they saw what was new and fashionable.
scenes.caption: WINDOW DRESSERS

scenes.text: Some stores also put on a Thanksgiving parade. Macy's in New York had been holding its parade since nineteen twenty-four, with giant balloons floating down Broadway. Hudson's in Detroit, Gimbels in Philadelphia and many other stores had parades of their own. At the very end came Santa Claus, which meant the Christmas shopping season had officially begun.
scenes.caption: THE THANKSGIVING PARADE

scenes.text: Through the revolving doors, you stepped onto the main floor. It was grand, with high ceilings, marble columns, chandeliers and glass counters that gleamed. It smelled of perfume, leather and fresh popcorn. The main floor was where the store put the things people bought on impulse. Cosmetics, jewelry, gloves, hats, scarves and handbags.
scenes.caption: THE MAIN FLOOR

scenes.text: Behind every counter stood a saleswoman in a neat dress, often a woman who had worked there for twenty years. She knew her merchandise and her customers. She'd help you find the right shade of lipstick, the right size glove, or the perfect gift for your mother. She wrote up the sale by hand, in a little book with carbon paper.
scenes.caption: THE SALESWOMAN

scenes.text: When you paid, the clerk might put your money and the sales slip into a little cylinder and send it whooshing through a pneumatic tube to the cashier's office. A minute later, it came whooshing back with your change and receipt. Children were fascinated by it. Some stores used those tube systems well into the sixties.
scenes.caption: THE PNEUMATIC TUBE

scenes.text: Many stores also had a beautiful clock, often hanging over the main floor or at the corner of the building. Meet me under the clock was a phrase everyone in town understood. Friends, sweethearts and families used it as a meeting place for generations. Marshall Field's clock in Chicago was so famous that it appeared on the cover of the Saturday Evening Post.
scenes.caption: MEET ME UNDER THE CLOCK

scenes.text: To go upstairs, you took the elevator. And in nineteen sixty-two, many department store elevators still had an operator. A young woman or an older man in a uniform with white gloves, who sat on a little stool, worked a brass lever, and called out each floor. Third floor, ladies' dresses, coats and lingerie. Going up.
scenes.caption: GOING UP

scenes.text: Some stores had escalators too, with wooden steps that clattered as they moved. Children loved riding them up and down. Mothers held small hands tightly at the top and bottom. And the escalator always seemed to deliver you right into the middle of something you didn't intend to buy.
scenes.caption: THE WOODEN ESCALATOR

scenes.text: The second and third floors were the fashion floors. Women's dresses, suits, coats and furs. In nineteen sixty-two, the look was elegant. Jackie Kennedy was the most admired woman in America, and women everywhere wanted her pillbox hats, simple sheath dresses and pearls. Stores sold copies of her outfits at every price.
scenes.caption: THE JACKIE KENNEDY LOOK

scenes.text: Shopping for clothes was a serious event. Women dressed up to go downtown, with hats, gloves and heels. Fitting rooms had attendants who brought you sizes. Alterations were done in the store, often for free. And many stores had a personal shopper, who could pick out a whole wardrobe for a busy customer.
scenes.query: 1960s woman trying on dress fitting room
scenes.caption: DRESSING UP TO SHOP

scenes.text: The men's department was often on the main floor or in a separate shop. Suits, sport coats, white shirts, ties and hats. A tailor measured a man for his suit with a tape measure and a piece of chalk. In nineteen sixty-two, a good suit might cost fifty to seventy-five dollars, and a man was expected to own at least two.
scenes.caption: THE MEN'S DEPARTMENT

scenes.text: Hats were a big business. In nineteen sixty-two, many women still bought a new hat every season, and the millinery department was full of feathers, veils and flowers. Men still wore fedoras, though that was changing fast. People said President Kennedy, who often went without a hat, helped bring the era of men's hats to an end.
scenes.caption: THE HAT DEPARTMENT

scenes.text: Children's clothing was usually on its own floor, along with shoes. Mothers came in late August for back-to-school clothes. Plaid dresses and saddle shoes for girls. Corduroy pants and button-down shirts for boys. And the shoe salesman measured your foot with a metal Brannock device, and maybe gave you a balloon.
scenes.caption: BACK TO SCHOOL

scenes.text: And then there was the toy department. In December, it took over a whole floor. Electric trains running on tracks around a mountain. Dolls in every size. Bicycles, sleds, games and chemistry sets. For a child in nineteen sixty-two, the toy department at Christmas might have been the most exciting place on Earth.
scenes.caption: THE TOY DEPARTMENT

scenes.text: And in the middle of it all sat Santa Claus, on a big throne in a little winter wonderland. The line to see him wound through the toy department. Children whispered their wishes, got a candy cane, and had their picture taken. Many families still have those photos, with a nervous child on Santa's lap, from the same store year after year.
scenes.caption: SANTA ON THE FIFTH FLOOR

scenes.text: Higher up were the home floors. Housewares, china, silver and linens. Brides registered for their wedding gifts here, choosing a china pattern and silver they would use for the rest of their lives. Furniture filled whole showrooms, arranged like living rooms and bedrooms. Appliances, televisions and stereos had their own department.
scenes.caption: THE BRIDAL REGISTRY

scenes.text: Many families bought their first good furniture at the downtown store, on credit. And that credit came with a charge plate. A little metal card, like a dog tag, embossed with your name and account number. The clerk pressed it into a machine to stamp the sales slip. Having a charge account at the big store downtown was a sign that you had arrived.
scenes.caption: THE CHARGE PLATE

scenes.text: And for families who couldn't pay all at once, there was layaway. You picked out a coat or a toy, put down a few dollars, and the store held it in the back. Every week or two, you came in and paid a little more. When it was paid off, it was yours. Many Christmas presents came home that way.
scenes.caption: LAYAWAY

scenes.text: Many stores also offered services that sound amazing today. Free delivery, often the same day or the next, by the store's own trucks. Gift wrapping at a special counter, with the store's name on the box. A beauty salon, a barber shop, a post office, a travel bureau and a place to check your coat and packages. You could spend the whole day there.
scenes.caption: FREE DELIVERY

scenes.text: At lunchtime, shoppers rode up to the top floor, to the tearoom. It was elegant, with white tablecloths, waitresses in uniforms, and sometimes a fashion show of models walking between the tables. Women met their friends for chicken salad, tomato aspic, popovers and a slice of cake. Some stores had a children's menu with sandwiches cut into shapes.
scenes.caption: THE TEAROOM

scenes.text: Many stores were famous for one special dish. Marshall Field's in Chicago served chicken pot pie in its Walnut Room, under a huge Christmas tree. Neiman Marcus served popovers with strawberry butter. Hudson's in Detroit had its Maurice salad. People still try to recreate those recipes at home today.
scenes.query: Marshall Field's Walnut Room Christmas tree
scenes.caption: THE WALNUT ROOM

scenes.text: And then there was the bargain basement. Down below the main floor, things were different. Lower prices, crowded tables, and piles of marked-down merchandise. Filene's Basement in Boston was the most famous. There, prices dropped automatically every week an item went unsold, and shoppers fought over wedding dresses on sale day.
scenes.caption: THE BARGAIN BASEMENT

scenes.text: For many working families, the basement was where they really shopped. Clothes for the children, towels, socks and everyday things. And everyone loved the thrill of finding a real treasure in the bins. A designer coat for a fraction of the price, or the perfect shoes for half off.
scenes.caption: THE THRILL OF THE HUNT

scenes.text: And the store's own box mattered. A gift in a Marshall Field's green box, a Neiman Marcus box or a Tiffany blue box told the person opening it that you had gone to the best store in town. Many people kept those boxes for years and reused them, so that even a homemade gift seemed a little fancier.
scenes.caption: THE STORE'S BOX

scenes.text: The department store was the heart of downtown, and downtown was the heart of the city. On a Saturday, families took the bus or the streetcar into town, or parked in the new parking garages. They shopped, ate lunch, saw a movie at the big theater, and maybe stopped at the bakery on the way home.
scenes.caption: THE HEART OF THE CITY

scenes.text: Every shopping trip was a social event. You ran into neighbors, friends from church and people from work. The doorman at the store knew your name. The streets were full of life, day and night. In nineteen sixty-two, going downtown felt like going somewhere.
scenes.caption: GOING SOMEWHERE

scenes.text: So what happened? The same thing that happened to Main Street. Families moved to the suburbs. Shopping malls opened on the edge of town, with free parking and air conditioning. Many department stores opened branches in the malls. And slowly, the downtown flagship lost its customers.
scenes.caption: THE MALLS

scenes.text: Through the seventies and eighties, many big downtown stores closed. Gimbels closed in nineteen eighty-six. Hudson's downtown Detroit store closed in nineteen eighty-three, and its building was imploded in nineteen ninety-eight. Then came mergers. Many beloved local names, like Marshall Field's, Filene's, Rich's and Wanamaker's, were turned into Macy's.
scenes.caption: THE NAMES DISAPPEARED

scenes.text: Today, many of those grand old buildings stand empty, or have been turned into apartments, offices or hotels. A few, like Macy's in Herald Square in New York, still open their doors every morning. And at Christmas, some still decorate their windows, and families still come downtown to see them.
scenes.caption: A FEW STILL REMAIN

scenes.text: Why do we miss them so much? Because the downtown department store was more than a place to buy things. It was a place to dress up, to see and be seen, to take the children to see Santa, and to have lunch with your mother in the tearoom. It made an ordinary Saturday feel special.
scenes.caption: IT MADE SATURDAY SPECIAL

scenes.text: If you remember the downtown department store, you remember the elevator operator, the Christmas windows, the charge plate and the tearoom. You remember holding your mother's hand on the escalator. Those stores are mostly gone. But for a generation of Americans, they were where the magic happened.
scenes.caption: WHERE THE MAGIC HAPPENED

scenes.text: So tell us in the comments. What was the name of your downtown department store? Did you visit Santa there, or eat in the tearoom? What did your family buy there? We read every comment. Next time, we're looking at what being a grandparent in nineteen sixty was really like. Thank you for spending this time with me.
scenes.caption: WHAT WAS YOUR STORE?
